title: A symptom-first method: narrow the layer in ten minutes
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Write one sentence that says who sees what, since when, how often and how bad.
Most incidents follow a change: a deployment, a configuration or flag change, a certificate or key expiry, a traffic shift, a dependency update or a quota limit.
A request travels through client, DNS, network, load balancer, application, dependencies and storage.
State a hypothesis that a test could disprove, such as if the pool is exhausted then waiting connections will be at the maximum.
If users are hurt, restore service before finding the root cause: roll back, fail over, scale out or disable a feature.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Twenty minutes of guessing
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
An error rate rose and three engineers tried different ideas at the same time.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl rollout history deploy/checkout -n shop | tail -2
Each engineer changed a different setting, so no one knew which change had any effect.
The incident lead stopped the changes and asked what changed.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Several people changing things at once.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Scenario: pods that will not start: Pending, image pull and crash loops
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A Pending pod has been accepted but not placed or started.
ErrImagePull means the node could not fetch the image, and ImagePullBackOff means it is waiting before retrying.
CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and exits repeatedly.
A liveness probe that fails restarts the container.
Pending leads to describe events.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The deployment that kept restarting
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A new version restarted every minute and the logs were empty after each restart.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl describe pod orders-6f7 -n shop | grep -A6 "Last State"
The previous logs showed that the container was loading a large cache at start.
The pod had a memory limit lower than the cache size, so the kernel killed it each time, and exit code 137 with OOMKilled confirmed it.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Reading current logs of a restarted container only.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Scenario: DNS and service discovery failures
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A pod uses the resolver settings in resolv.conf, which point to the cluster DNS service and list search domains.
The ndots option says how many dots a name needs before it is tried as absolute.
CoreDNS serves cluster names and forwards others to upstream resolvers.
Occasional five second delays can come from lost UDP packets, connection tracking races on busy nodes, or a single bad upstream among several.
In clouds a private zone returns internal addresses only to linked networks.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Slow calls to a payment provider
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Calls to an external API took five seconds in about one case in twenty.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl exec deploy/checkout -n shop -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
Each lookup of the external name first tried the cluster suffixes, and some of those queries were lost on a busy node, so the resolver waited for its five second timeout before retrying.
The team lowered ndots for that workload, used a fully qualified name, enabled a node local cache and added an alert on the CoreDNS latency.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Not testing DNS first in a slow service.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Scenario: intermittent 502, 503 and 504 behind a load balancer
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A 502 means the balancer got an invalid or no response from a backend, often because a connection was closed.
Read the balancer access log fields that show the balancer status, the backend status and the timings.
If the balancer reuses a connection that the backend has already closed because of its own idle timeout, the next request fails with a 502 at random.
During a deployment, a pod that is stopped while still in the target list receives requests that fail.
A backend that reaches its worker or connection limit queues requests, and the balancer times out.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Random 502s every few minutes
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
About half a percent of requests returned 502 with no pattern in the application logs.
An operator runs a command such as: grep ' 502 ' lb-access.log | head -1
The application server closed idle connections after five seconds, while the balancer kept them for sixty.
Whenever a request was sent on a connection that had just been closed, the balancer logged a 502 with no backend status.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Backend idle timeout shorter than the balancer.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Scenario: slower after a deploy: pools, garbage collection, locks and neighbours
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Compare the same endpoint before and after, at the same traffic level, using p50, p95 and p99.
Use a trace for a slow request and read the spans: time in the application, in each dependency and waiting.
A connection pool or thread pool that is too small makes requests wait, and one that is too large overloads the database.
In managed runtimes, long or frequent pauses add to the tail.
A new lock in a hot path serialises requests.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: p99 tripled after a harmless change
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A release that changed only a cache key format made the 99th percentile latency three times worse.
An operator runs a command such as: curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep -E "cache_(hits|misses)_total"
The new key format did not match the keys already stored, and a bug added a random part to each key, so almost every lookup missed and went to the database.
The database became the queue, and the tail latency rose.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Comparing at different traffic levels.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Scenario: cloud API failures: access denied, quotas and throttling
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: An access denied can come from the identity policy, a resource policy, a permission boundary, an organisation level deny, a missing condition such as region or tag, or an expired credential.
Accounts have limits on instances, addresses, rules and API rates, and these are per region.
Cloud APIs rate limit callers and return errors such as too many requests.
Some services need a short time before a new resource or policy is visible everywhere.
Search the audit log for the failing call around the time of the error.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The deploy that failed only in one region
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A pipeline deployed successfully in two regions and failed in the third with an authorisation error.
An operator runs a command such as: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=RunInstances --max-resu
The audit event named an explicit deny in an organisation policy that allowed only approved regions, and the third region was not on the list.
The pipeline role itself was correct, so editing it would never have helped.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Editing the identity policy when a higher layer denies.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
